2027-07-27.title: Tuesday of the tenth week after Pentecost
readings: We walk by faith, not by sight, and make it our aim to please the Lord
The barren fig tree: the gardener asks for one more year
2027-07-27.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Tenth Sunday after Pentecost. No commemoration is printed in the Panchangam today. The Malayalam month of Karkidakam, the month of the heaviest rain, is under way.
2027-07-27.verse: for we walk by faith, not by sight.
theo: St Paul is writing about confidence, and the odd thing is that he is writing from a place where nothing can be seen. “So we are always confident; even though we know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord; for we walk by faith, not by sight.” Anyone who has crossed a flooded paddy field at night along the narrow bund will know what he means. You cannot see the whole path; a small lamp shows the next step and the next, and you walk because you trust that the ground is there. Faith is that walk. Paul is not despising the body, which God made and will raise; he is saying that, as long as we live in it, we know the Lord by trust and not yet by sight, and that this is enough for courage. Because the end is the Lord, he gives life a single aim: “whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him.” And he adds a sober reminder: “For all of us must appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive recompense for what has been done in the body, whether good or evil.” We do not meet a stranger there. We meet the Christ who loved us and gave himself for us.

The Gospel puts a picture beside the aim to please him: a fig tree planted in a vineyard, which the owner has watched for three years and found without fruit. “Cut it down! Why should it be wasting the soil?” In our own compounds the picture is easy to see: a jackfruit or mango tree that gets the best of the soil and the rain and never bears. The tree is every one of us, and the soil that it wastes is the time, the gifts and the grace that God has given. Jesus told this parable immediately after speaking of repentance, when he said that unless people repent they will all perish (Luke 13:1–5). The fruit that he looks for is a changed life: the fruit of the Spirit, which is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, generosity, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control.

Then the gardener speaks, and the whole story turns on his voice: “Sir, let it alone for one more year, until I dig around it and put manure on it. If it bears fruit next year, well and good; but if not, you can cut it down.” The Church has long heard in these words the voice of Christ, who stands between us and judgment and asks for time. He does not ask the owner to ignore the barren tree; he promises to work: to dig around it, loosen the hard ground and feed it. And note what he feeds it with: the manure. God does not waste even the refuse of our lives, our failures and our humiliations; in his hands they become what makes us fruitful. The one more year is today, for “now is the acceptable time; see, now is the day of salvation!” In the lean, rainy weeks of Karkidakam our grandparents used to say that the tree you tend now feeds the house next year. Let us not waste the year that the Lord asks for us.
outline: Ask: if the owner of the vineyard came to my life today, what fruit would he find?
A small lamp for the next step: trust in the Lord, whom we do not yet see.
Point 2 · Our aim to please him
Whether at home or away, we aim to please the Lord, before whose judgment seat we all stand.
The gardener asks for time, digs and feeds the tree; the time is now.
Let the Gardener work on you today.
live: Take the next step by faith (2 Corinthians 5:7)
Choose one decision you have delayed because you cannot see the whole road, and take its first step today in prayer.
Name one fruit of the Spirit that is missing in you, patience or kindness for example, and practise it with one person today.
2027-07-27.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you are the Gardener who asks for one more year for each of us. Give us the faith to walk when we cannot see, and the aim to please you in all things. Dig around our hardness, feed us with your grace, and make us bear the fruit of love, so that when we stand before your judgment seat we may hear: Well done. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono faith sees what the eyes cannot: the bread and the wine are the Body and Blood of Christ, and the fruit of his sacrifice feeds us so that we may bear fruit that lasts.

quick: St Paul says that we walk by faith, not by sight, and that our aim is to please the Lord.
All of us must appear before the judgment seat of Christ, who loved us and gave himself for us.
In the parable the gardener asks the owner for one more year for the barren fig tree, and promises to dig around it and feed it.
2027-07-27.action: Take one small step of faith today, even though you cannot see the whole road.
2027-07-27.question: If the owner of the vineyard came to my life today, what fruit would he find?

family.explain: A man planted a fig tree and waited for fruit, but the tree gave none for three years. He wanted to cut it down, but the gardener said, “Please give it one more year. I will dig around it and give it food.” Jesus is like that gardener. He is patient with us and gives us time, and he helps us to grow good fruit: love, kindness and patience.
family.intention: We pray that we may use the time God gives us to grow in love.
family.ask: Ask: “What good fruit can I grow this week: kindness, patience or sharing?”

illus: An old woman in a village near Kottarakkara had a mango tree behind her house that had flowered every year and never given a mango. Her son wanted to cut it for firewood. She said, “Give it one more year.” That year she dug around its roots, put ash and cow dung at the foot, watered it through the summer, and talked to it as she walked past. In the monsoon the following year it hung with mangoes. Asked how she had known, she answered, “I did not know. I only knew that I had not yet done everything for it.” The people who heard her told it afterwards as a parable about God.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, patient Gardener, give us time and grace to bear fruit. Teach us to walk by faith and to make it our aim to please you. Amen.
share: We walk by faith, not by sight (2 Corinthians 5:7). When has trust carried me through when I could not see the way?
Whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him (2 Corinthians 5:9). What would it mean to make this my aim this week?
Let it alone for one more year (Luke 13:8). Where has the Lord been patient with me?
pm.resp: Lord, make us bear good fruit.
interc: For the Church, that she may bear the fruit of love in every land and in every season.
For farmers and gardeners in this season of rain, that the fields may be fruitful and the harvest blessed.
For all who feel they have wasted their lives, that they may hear the Gardener asking for one more year.
For the dying, that they may be at home with the Lord in peace.
For ourselves, that we may make it our aim to please the Lord in all things.
pm.close: Father, you are patient and you do not want anyone to perish. Give us a year, a day, an hour in which to bear fruit; dig around our hardness and feed us with your grace, that we may walk by faith and please you in all things. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, St Paul tells us that we walk by faith, not by sight (2 Corinthians 5:7). Think of crossing a flooded field at night with a small lamp. You see only the next step, and you walk because you trust that the ground is there. Faith is that walk. And Paul gives life a single aim: whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him (2 Corinthians 5:9).

He adds a sober reminder: all of us must appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10). But the judge is the Christ who loved us and gave himself for us. The question is not how to escape him but how to be ready to meet him.

The Gospel gives a picture: a fig tree that has borne no fruit for three years. The owner says, Cut it down. The gardener says, Sir, let it alone for one more year, until I dig around it and put manure on it (Luke 13:8). Jesus is that gardener. He gives us time, and he digs and feeds us with his grace. Even the refuse of our lives he turns into nourishment.

So let us not waste the year he asks for us. Now is the acceptable time; now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2). Let us take one step by faith today, and let us bear one fruit of the Spirit. Amen.
kids: Children, do you have a tree at home, a mango or a jackfruit or a coconut? Think how long it takes for a tree to give fruit! A man in Jesus' story had a fig tree that gave no fruit for three years. He wanted to cut it down, but the gardener said, “Give it one more year. I will take care of it.” Jesus is like that gardener. He is patient with us, he helps us grow, and he wants us to bear good fruit: kindness, sharing and love. What good fruit will you grow this week?

concl: We walk by faith, not by sight, with the single aim of pleasing the Lord who will be our judge and who loves us.
The Gardener asks for one more year and works at our roots; today is that year.
